segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: One of the producers of our radio program, Sean Cole, used to live in Toronto. And he went out to bars a lot when he was there. And at one point, he heard this rumor about the places that he was hanging out.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: A friend of mine basically said, the thing about these bars-- he actually said, the gasoline that allows them to function was cocaine.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Meaning the staff was doing cocaine?

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: The bartenders were on coke. And I was like, how did I not notice? You know?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: And I wondered how true that was.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Did you do any coke tonight?

segments.speaker: Bartender 1
segments.text: Yeah. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: How much?

segments.speaker: Bartender 1
segments.text: Just a bump.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: So that's like, what is that.

segments.speaker: Bartender 1
segments.text: That's like the tip of a key.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: So this is one of about a dozen bartenders that I interviewed, all anonymously.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When she says a key, she means like--

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Like a house key. You sniff it off of that.

segments.speaker: Bartender 1
segments.text: But I have done it while I'm working. But I don't do it until later, like past 1:00.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Oh, I see.

segments.speaker: Bartender 1
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: And how often does that happen?

segments.speaker: Bartender 1
segments.text: Umm, like, every weekend.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I had this experience years ago. A friend sat me down and told me that she'd just started going to AA. And she wanted me to know that she knew how annoying it must have been for me and all of our friends at the time that she was always on coke back when we first were getting to know each other.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She was running to the bathroom all the time. She was really hyper. And I told her, I had no idea. I told her, I just assumed that's your personality. You're a little manic, small bladder. And of course, right?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I think, if you're not a daily drug user, you're not a big drug user, it doesn't occur to you that the people around you might be high. And Sean found that this bar scene he thought he knew so well did, actually, seem to be run on cocaine.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: So lots of bars in certain areas of town, definitely, coke is like fuel for the staff. Partly because, you know, these bars, it's like drinking on the job is kind of expected.

segments.speaker: Bartender 2
segments.text: People are buying me shots. And I see people I know, and I'm buying them shots. And then, just, you start to get the spins.

segments.speaker: Bartender 1
segments.text: It's like, after you do four or five shots, I'm like, OK. I don't want to be too drunk. I need something to straighten me up.

segments.speaker: Bartender 2
segments.text: Jeez, I really want a line right now to straighten this up.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: That's the phrase you keep hearing.

segments.speaker: Bartender 3
segments.text: Everyone uses it so loosely. It's straightening out. You need to straighten out.

segments.speaker: Bartender 2
segments.text: Yeah, you just take a quick little jump down to the bathroom, straighten yourself up. Come upstairs.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: How often does that happen to you?

segments.speaker: Bartender 2
segments.text: Uh, eight minutes ago.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Bartender 2
segments.text: [LAUGHS] Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So their bosses have to know, right?

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: The bosses are doing it too sometimes.

segments.speaker: Bartender 3
segments.text: For the first little while, the bar I worked at, the managers were doing lines of cocaine in order to sober up enough so they could cash out the bartenders, who were completely inebriated. Oh! I also knew policemen who were partaking.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: In cocaine?

segments.speaker: Bartender 3
segments.text: In the bathroom, with the manager, in uniform. It blew me away! I was so naive. I was like, what? It would be like finding out Superman is-- you know--

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Doing cocaine.

segments.speaker: Bartender 3
segments.text: --doing cocaine! Exactly.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Of course, to put it in perspective, this is a cop doing cocaine in a city whose mayor was caught on video smoking crack and stayed in his job. He's finally going to rehab now. And all of this got us thinking here at the radio show, how many people around us are high right now? Like, right this second?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, if you're out in the world right now as you're hearing me say these words, look around at the people around you. Look at their faces. Could one of them be high? And I mean, everywhere you go, right? It's like, for example, we found this book that came out a couple of years ago by a guy named Ethan Bryson.

segments.speaker: Dr. Ethan Bryson
segments.text: So the title of the book is Addicted Healers. And the subtitle is "5 Key Signs Your Healthcare Professional May Be Drug Impaired."

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: And right here on page xviii, it says, "Rates of illicit drug use by health care professionals within the past year ranged from 8% to 20%, depending on the type of personnel within the health care industry." And then, it says, "At any given time, roughly 3% to 5% of this population is using illicit drugs while they are caring for patients."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: 3% to 5%, you mean of all health care professionals?

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: All across the profession.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wow, which drugs?

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: They all have their drug of choice. And we actually played this kind of word association game.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Physicians?

segments.speaker: Dr. Ethan Bryson
segments.text: Pills, Oxycontin, oxycodone.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Nurses.

segments.speaker: Dr. Ethan Bryson
segments.text: Intravenous opioid-based drugs.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Psychiatrists.

segments.speaker: Dr. Ethan Bryson
segments.text: Benzodiazepines.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Anesthesiologists.

segments.speaker: Dr. Ethan Bryson
segments.text: Fentanyl.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: You said that so fast!

segments.speaker: Dr. Ethan Bryson
segments.text: That is the biggest drug.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: I should point out here that Dr. Bryson is himself an anesthesiologist.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Say it again, fentanyl?

segments.speaker: Dr. Ethan Bryson
segments.text: Fentanyl. It's a highly potent derivative of morphine.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: It's actually like 80 times more potent than morphine and can significantly mess with your judgment. It's extremely addictive. And Dr. Bryson pointed out that most medical professionals don't have to take drug tests. Military personnel, on the other hand, do.

segments.speaker: Deborah Lee James
segments.text: Now, many of you reported last week on the investigation involving some of our airmen and illegal drug possession.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: This is the Secretary of the Air Force, Deborah Lee James, giving a press conference a few months ago. Basically, two lieutenants were busted for allegedly dealing amphetamines and ecstasy. And they were found out, because they were sending text messages to other airmen about drugs.

segments.speaker: Deborah Lee James
segments.text: Well, it turns out that three of the 10 who were implicated in this drug investigation were from our Air Force Global Strike Command, which is the command where our ICBM missile forces reside.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: ICBM, that is--

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: The nuclear warheads.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, that doesn't seem like somebody we want high.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Not someone we want high.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Sean, are there surveys measuring how many of us are high all the time?

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: I mean-- [SIGH] There's not a lot of data. There's workplace drug tests that show 3 and 1/2% of workers test positive for drugs. But obviously, that's only in workplaces that test for drugs in the first place.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: One of the experts on this data, who's wonderfully named, Dr. Barry Sample from Quest Diagnostics told me drug use is a couple percentage points higher in places that don't test for drugs.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Which jobs have the highest drug use?

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: So, the Department of Health and Human Services actually has numbers on that. The latest ones that I found said-- so this is people who say, yes, I've done illicit drugs in the past month. People who work in real estate is about 7%. Same for mining.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Mining? 7%.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Mining. Retail is 9 and 1/2%. Construction workers is about 14%. So that means roughly one in seven construction workers. The highest is accommodation and food services.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That would include, dare I say, bartenders? [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Yes. Accommodation and food services, roughly one in six admit on the survey to using drugs.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It could be higher, though, right?

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: It could be higher? What do you mean?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It could be higher than one of six actually do drugs.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Oh, it could be higher--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Right, one out of six--

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: --meaning one out of six admit on the survey--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: --admit on the survey to drug use. Some more of them, actually, might be doing it.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Yeah, maybe.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They should try the survey in Toronto.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, today on our radio program, the secret world of getting high, which is, OK, maybe not such a well-kept secret. It is all around us all the time. High people mingling with us, working, passing, laughing extra hard at our jokes. We don't even know why.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We have stories today of great drug experiences, and awful drug experiences, and funny drug experiences; tales of miscalculation, bad judgment, and dumb-assery. We have comedians Marc Maron and Wyatt Cenac. From WBEZ Chicago, It's This American Life, distributed by Public Radio International. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act One, High on the Corporate Ladder. So there's this secret society, many million strong, people who are going through life high. Maybe you are part of this society. If not, you're probably dealing regularly with people who are, cashiers, baristas, and stockbrokers, and cab drivers, maybe the cop writing that parking ticket. Alex Blumberg has this story about just how hard it is to tell who is in that society and who isn't.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Richard, for many years, was a member of that society, the society of people who get high at work.

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: I would roll a thin joint and start smoking in the morning. I'd usually duck down at one of the back stairways and take a few more tokes during the day. I'd smoke at lunch. I'd smoke a little bit in the afternoon. I would basically stay high all day long.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And what exactly was your job title?

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: I was chief operating [LAUGHS] officer of the second largest ad agency in town. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: [LAUGHS] How many people at your company knew that you were doing this?

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: Um, somewhere between three and all of them.

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Richard says that, at the time, he thought he was hiding his habit. But in retrospect, who knows? One of the head executives toking up in the stairwell every day, how could he hide that? On the other hand, there's this. I had no idea that this was going  on. And I'm Richard's son.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: I only found out that my dad was getting high at work every day long after the fact, when I was in my 30s. And I found out because my dad got cancer. It was a horrible week. It started with the discovery that the pain in my dad's back wasn't just a pinched nerve. And it ended with a diagnosis of lymphoma, a particular form of lymphoma that we had learned that week to root for, because it's actually curable. That's the word they used. Back then, I didn't even know you could say that about cancer.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: But that whole week, my dad was convinced he had a different diagnosis, lung cancer. Even towards the end, when the doctors were pretty convinced the news was good, he insisted on it, which didn't make any sense. My father had quit smoking cigarettes way back in the '80s.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: When we pressed him about it, that's when he told us about the pot. My dad's cancer and recovery was a pivotal time for our family. Painful secrets came out. Much was said that needed to be said. My dad got into a 12-step program. And he's been clean for almost 15 years.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: But then, here at the radio show, someone suggested doing a show called "I was so high," and I realized something. I really wanted us to do that show. I had a lot of questions for people who got high all day, questions about what they thought of themselves, what they thought of their families, what they were getting out of being high. I realized, in other words, I had a lot of questions for my dad.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: When did you use marijuana for the first time?

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: Uh, I don't know. You were about a year and a half old.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: First, of course, I wanted the details. When did it start? When did it get serious? And for my dad, it started in the '60s. A friend rolled a joint at a party. It was fun. It became something he did socially, getting high with friends, listening to Jefferson Airplane on the brand new FM station in town.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And this part I knew. I remember joints passed around when my parents' friends came over, rolling papers on the end table next to the couch. One afternoon, I answered the door and found a friend of my dad's, turtleneck, sunglasses, what I remember as a Burt Reynolds mustache. He handed me a dime-bag and said, this is for your father.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: My dad doesn't remember the first time he smoked weed at work. But it was probably around the time I was leaving middle school and entering high school. By the time I left for college, it had gone far beyond a thing he did at nights with friends to a thing he did routinely, during the day, while he'd walk the several blocks to a meeting with one of his firm's largest clients.

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: I knew where every alleyway between our office on Seventh Street and Procter, on the other corner of downtown.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And you're talking about a meeting with Procter & Gamble--

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: --one of the largest companies in the world. That was one of clients. If there's any company less associated with habitual work-time pot use, it has to Procter & Gamble.

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: So, when you were making these presentations, you don't think that they knew that you were high at the time? That you'd stopped in at an alley on the way over and smoked a joint?

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: No. I was putting something over on the straight world.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Like, I'm not really part of your world. I'm just visiting here for a little bit.

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: I think that was something that was very, very much a part of being stoned. Here I was, this guy in a business suit, tucking down a back alley and smoking a joint.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Another question I had for my dad, were there people for whom his drug use was not a secret? Other members of the Society of Secret Pot Smokers that he'd duck into that alley with? Was he regularly sharing joints with-- I don't know-- the Kinko's guy while they both waited on a large print order?

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: I could see a camaraderie developing between secret pot smokers, just like cigarette smokers at an office will go out and take smoke breaks together. But my dad says that, for him at least, it wasn't like that. Sure, he knew of other people at the agency who smoked pot. And yes, if you must know, they were mostly in the art department. But he mainly kept to himself.

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: You increasing live in a secret world that you can't reveal to the people who don't share that world. And there are an increasingly limited number of people who share the world-- the more you use, the deeper you get into it, to the point where you're all alone in it. And you have to keep it a secret from everybody else. And you do really stupid things to keep it a secret, really stupid.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: What are you thinking of when you said "really stupid"?

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: Well, I remember one time, I went down, I'd stopped in Eton Park on the way back to the office. And I got out of the car. And I got stoned. I smoked a joint. And I came back, and I realized that I'd locked my keys in the car. And I couldn't-- you know, I was stoned. My judgment was shot. I didn't know what to do.

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: So I went around. And I found a big rock. And I broke the little window in the rear. And I reached in and unlocked the door. And then, the back of the seat was full of glass. And I had to go down to Ace Auto Glass and had the glass replaced. And then, finally, I got to the office an hour and a half late for the meeting. And I made up some excuse. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: This image of my dad in his suit, early morning, rooting around in the underbrush for a rock to throw through his own car window, I found it so shocking. It is one solution to the problem at hand. But it's hard to imagine a person who wasn't high, weighing all the options and deciding, you know the think I need to do right now at 8:00 AM on a work day? Smash in my own car window.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And I know, as rock bottom stories go, this is nothing special. In general, my dad's addiction story barely registers on the family dysfunction scale. But his marijuana use was starting to fray the edges of his life. He and his business partner, Dale, were having regular fights over my dad's inability to show up to meetings on time, or fill out his time sheets, or just get things done when he said he would.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: At a certain point, my dad sold his stake in the business for a nice chunk of money. But then, he lost most of it on a string of failed business ventures. I remember my dad trying to explain a couple of them to me at the time. I was just out of college at this point. And I never really understood what the products actually were or how they were going to make any money.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Only in retrospect did I realize, after the cancer and the secret came out, those business ideas, they made a lot more sense if you were stoned. All told, in today's dollars, my dad probably lost somewhere north of half a million. And this brings me to the most basic question I had for my dad, the question that lay underneath all the other ones.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Why do you think you were getting high every day at work?

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: Uh, I think that I was getting high because I didn't really feel that marketing was a worthwhile thing to do.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: This is part of it for sure. Getting high allowed my dad to retreat from this reality that he didn't want to face, that he wasn't a hippie anymore but, in fact, a guy in a suit with a job in advertising.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: But that answer, it didn't feel like the full truth to me. Because he wasn't just running from reality at work. He was running from it at home as well.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: The one time in particular I remember was we were on vacation out in California. It was one of the times we went to California. We did a big road trip across the country. It was sort of crazy.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And we'd found some unbelievably beautiful little swimming hole in northern California. And we'd set up a tent. And the weather was perfect. And we were all getting out. We'd put on our swimsuits. And we were all getting ready to get in. And we'd just been visiting your friends Gene and Jan in San Francisco. And they'd given you some--

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: They'd given you some Berkeley gold, as they called it.

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And I remember you rolling a joint and saying something like, but first, it's time for little Berkeley gold, or something like that. And I remember being really upset. And part of, I think, the reason that I was so upset is I remember thinking, what in the world? What more could you want?

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And there's sort of a feeling of, are we not enough? It seemed like, almost even at that time in your life, you were almost sort of running from something even in that moment or wanting to change the reality a little bit in that moment. Is it--

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: I think I probably was.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: What were you--? What didn't you have?

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: I don't know.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: I don't know what it was. I had a perfect life.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: I guess that's where I feel like I go back to it was feeling. Like, I find when I've used pot, the thing that it takes away is it takes away feeling.

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: Yep.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Feelings become less intense. And I feel like, for whatever reason, the feelings of oh my god, this is so perfect. I love my family so much. Or, oh my god, this should be so perfect, but I'm pissed off at my wife. Or, I'm let down by my children, or whatever it is that you were feeling. I sort of feel like that's the thing that links all of the pot use. Is that true? Or is that just my theory?

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: Yeah, I think it's true. It's part of what you're running away from. The most important thing is that you're running away from something. You're running away from looking at the world as it really is. You push all of that direct experience of reality away. It's not a good way to live. It's just not a good way to live.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Oddly, for my dad, it wasn't just the happy moments he regretted checking out for, but the sad ones as well. For example, when his mother died of cancer. My aunt had been telling my dad that their mother's condition was getting worse, worse than their mother was letting on.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: If my dad hadn't been high, he says, he wouldn't have ignored what my aunt was telling him. He would have spent more time with his mother, engaged more with her doctors.

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: I probably would have been in Cleveland with her when she had the operation that ended in her death.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Oh, I didn't know that she died during operation.

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: Yes. She had bone cancer. And they were trying to break a connection to the pituitary gland or something like that that would reduce the pain. And she wound up hemorrhaging and died.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Mm. And you thought about going with her when she did that and you decided not to?

segments.speaker: Richard
segments.text: If it were to happen today, there's no question that I would have driven her up to Cleveland. That would've been the most natural thing in the world to do.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Instead, he says, he got high, pushed the feelings aside, and avoided the whole thing, which makes this last story I'll tell all the more amazing. Just last month, my 80-year-old Uncle Paul, my mom's brother, fell ill suddenly and ended up in the hospital, near death, with a breathing tube down his throat.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: My parents got the call and were on a plane down to Florida where he lived the very next day. My uncle was a recluse. Except for occasional phone calls to his brothers and sisters, he interacted with almost no one. It was my parents and a neighbor that Paul barely knew confronting the sad end to his lonely life, Medicaid applications, power of attorney, hospice, finally, cremation.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And while my parents were down there going about all that, my dad did something that was, on the one hand, utterly ordinary, but that I found remarkable. He emailed us with regular, almost daily, updates, giving the details on Paul's changing condition, going through next steps. The emails were direct and honest, filled with love for Paul and sadness about his decline.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: And I would sit there and read them. And they felt miraculous. A daily email on a tough, hard-to-face topic from my dad, something he never could have done organizationally or emotionally when he was high.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: Like I said, as these stories go, ours wasn't that bad. My dad was a good dad. He read to us every night, took us on long hikes in search of snakes and salamanders to keep as pets. But his drug use did leave at least one lasting effect on me. I can't hear any story about a seemingly functional pot-head with anything but a skeptical ear.

segments.speaker: Alex Blumberg
segments.text: From magazine features about rappers who are constantly high but still put out platinum records to casual asides about this friend I know who smokes weed all day but is a great husband and father, some part of me just can't buy it, can't help but think, there's more to that story. There's always something being run from. And there's always at least one person wondering, is that something me?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Alex Blumberg is one of the producers of our show. Coming up, Marc Maron, Wyatt Cenac and what do you say to Drew Carey when you are a contestant on The Price is Right and you're also high on mushrooms? That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio and Public Radio International when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life from Ira Glass. Each weekend our program, of course. We choose a theme, bring you different kinds of stories on that theme. segments.speaker: Ira Glass

segments.text: Well, being the people that can function in this society that we're supposed to sort of function in.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, I feel like you get so quickly, in this kind of discussion, to there are just two different ways to drink or do drugs. And there's all the people who can't control it. And they end up alcoholics and addicts. And then, there's all the people who can control it. They can do it occasionally, and they're fine. And it's just--

segments.speaker: Marc Maron
segments.text: Those horrible people.

segments.speaker: Marc Maron
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Marc Maron
segments.text: Those horrible people that can have a couple of drinks. Or even worse, the people like, yeah, I smoke a couple of cigarettes, maybe, on the weekend. You horrible person! Where's your sense of commitment?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Marc Maron
segments.text: I mean, don't you want to invest your life in this project? OK.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I want to play you a clip of you. This is you performing in 1998. I think you're just off drugs at this point. But maybe not.

segments.speaker: Marc Maron
segments.text: In all honesty, I feel bad for people who have never been addicted to anything. Because they're the real losers.

segments.speaker: Marc Maron
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Marc Maron
segments.text: You want to know why? Because they just don't know what it's like to really want something-- and get it again, and again, and again--

segments.speaker: Marc Maron
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Marc Maron
segments.text: [APPLAUSE]

segments.speaker: Marc Maron
segments.text: --until their sick and have to stop.

segments.speaker: Marc Maron
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Marc Maron
segments.text: That's passion.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Do you still feel that way?

segments.speaker: Marc Maron
segments.text: Yeah. [LAUGHS] I feel that way as a survivor. And it's very hard for me to say-- like, I don't regret the times I did drugs. I don't regret the times that I almost died or was in horrible situations. I don't regret wasting, possibly, years of my life. Because I can't live like that. I can't live in those regrets.

segments.speaker: Marc Maron
segments.text: But some of those times were great times. Some of those times were hilarious times. I don't regret all those times. I mean, am I happy that it didn't drag me down the hole? And hurt a lot of other people? And make me sick in a way that I could not get better or even die? I'm happy about that. But I am also thrilled that I had some of the experiences I did. And that's the two sides of it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Marc Maron. The second season of his TV show on IFC starts May 8.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Five, "DEA Agent Takes a Hit." So this is a moment when everything seems in flux in how our country sees and deals with drugs, particularly marijuana. Case in point, the past few months in Congress, the House Government Oversight Committee has been holding a series of hearings called "Mixed Signals, the Administration's Stance on Marijuana."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: These are the Committee's first hearings on pot in a decade. And they're holding them now, in large part, because so many states-- 20 states plus Washington, DC-- now allow some form of legal marijuana, which of course is in direct conflict with federal drug law. And one of the interesting things about these hearings is that two congressmen who think that our marijuana policies are totally out of whack, they think that pot should not be illegal under federal law-- have been using these hearings as an opportunity to, basically, lay into narcs, just to chew them out.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's kind of incredible. You almost never hear people on two sides of this issue talk to each other this directly, this fiercely, in public. One side, OK, sees pot smoking as normal, everyday, no biggie. What's the fuss? The other side sees the everyday-ness of pot as the problem, as a menace. Brian Reed tells about one of these congressional face-offs.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: I'm going to play you my favorite tape from these hearings. It's of one of the congressmen, Steve Cohen from Memphis in an Oversight Committee hearing on March 4. Cohen isn't even on the Oversight Committee, by the way.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: He asked for special permission to take part in the hearing, because he had some things he wanted to say to the witness, Thomas Harrigan. Harrigan is second in charge of the agency tasked with enforcing federal drug laws, the DEA. The two men do not see eye-to-eye.

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: Mr. Harrigan, you've been in this business now for close to 30 years? 1987, you started with the DEA. How have your views changed on marijuana in those 30 years?

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: To be quite honest with you, sir, very little.

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: I was afraid of that.

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: I see the devastation--

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: That's enough. The fact that it's changed very little says a lot about--

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: Do you want me to respond to your question, sir?

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: No, sir.

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: Because I would be happy to.

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: I know you would. We have limited time. The fact that it's changed very little shows that you haven't kept up with society. You haven't kept up with science. And it's part of the problem--

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: Science and medical I do keep up, sir.

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: All right. You mentioned in your statement that, quote, "It insults our common values." I want you to read me what you said.

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: Yes, sir. I believe this is the section you're referring to. "We also know that marijuana destroys lives and families, undermines our economy, and insults our common values."

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: What are the common values it insults?

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: For me, sir?

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: No, for--

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: I will tell you. I will tell you if you let me.

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: You said, we know. You're speaking as clairvoyant voice of America. What are our common values?

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: Well, I would venture to guess all of law enforcement, just about every single parent out there as well.

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: Every single parent?

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: Yes, every single parent. It's based on, again, medical, sir, and scientific fact, not public opinion. OK, I am not the medical expert, as I said before. Everything that I do is based on my 30 plus years of law enforcement.

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: Let me stop you for a minute. You said, it insults our common values. What is the value it insults?

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: What is the value it insults?

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: Yeah, you said, this--

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: Do we have all--? I could easily go on and on.

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: You haven't started yet.

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: Well, you continue to interrupt me. I would be happy to address your question.

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: Answer my question, sir.

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: Yes, you know what? From a bare minimum, as a parent, as a former educator, as a law enforcement official for all these years, I have seen the devastation that marijuana has caused not only on individuals, on families and communities.

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: What's our common value, though? You still haven't stated the common value. And the fact is 55% of Americans are in favor of decriminalization or legalization. I got to imagine that some of them are parents.

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: Your statement that all parents are against this is ludicrous. Want do you think? People that are in favor of decriminalization or a change in policy--

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: I didn't say, all.

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: --don't procreate?

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: I said, most parents--

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: You said, all.

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: --would be opposed to this.

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: And most is wrong too, 55% of America!

segments.speaker: Thomas Harrigan
segments.text: Are they all parents?

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: I don't think that the polls went into that. But I suspect a whole bunch of them were. It's not--

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: This went on for more than five minutes.

segments.speaker: Steve Cohen
segments.text: Let's get beyond Richard Nixon.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: I call the DEA to see if Thomas Harrigan wanted to come on the radio and have a chance to actually respond, since Cohen barely let him get a word in edgewise. But the DEA spokesperson said Harrigan was busy preparing for another hearing this week, so he couldn't do it.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: As for Congressman Cohen, one of his biggest beefs with the country's drug policy is the fact that marijuana is classified as a Schedule 1 drug. That means, in the eyes of the federal government , marijuana has a high potential for abuse and no accepted medical use.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Heroin, LSD, peyote, these are all Schedule 1. Cocaine and meth, on the other hand, are Schedule 2, a less serious designation. So under federal law, marijuana is considered the most dangerous type of drug, more dangerous than cocaine and meth. In Cohen's words, that's poppycock. He says, marijuana is the least dangerous of these drugs and most people know it including, apparently, President Obama.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: In a New Yorker profile earlier this year, Obama said, quote, "As has been well-documented, I smoked pot as a kid. And I view it as a bad habit and a vice, not very different from the cigarettes that I smoked as a young person up through a big chunk of my adult life. I don't think it is more dangerous than alcohol."

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: In fact, Obama said, quote, "In terms of its impact on the individual consumer, he believes pot is less dangerous than alcohol," which just shows how confused we are as a country right now when it comes to what we're supposed to be doing about marijuana. You've got the president of the United States saying something like that about pot while, at the same time, he's the boss of an entire bureaucracy with thousands of people whose job is to think the opposite.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Brian Reed is one of the producers of our show.

segments.text: Just hang on, man. Just hang on.
